```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5,
                      eval = requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE) &&
                        requireNamespace("spdep", quietly = TRUE) &&
                        requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE))
```

stareal maps prevalence from survey data, for example the share of
infections carrying a drug-resistance marker, on a set of areal units
(districts, counties, grid cells) and a regular time grid (months,
quarters, years). It estimates every area in every time step, with
uncertainty, including those that were never surveyed, and aggregates the
estimates to coarser groupings such as regions or countries.

This vignette runs through a complete analysis on simulated data, where
the truth is known. The [tutorials](https://mrc-ide.github.io/stareal/) on the
package website work through real analyses: the chloroquine-resistance
marker crt K76T across the Greater Horn of Africa, an emerging
artemisinin partial-resistance marker, covariates, cross-validation and
simulation studies. The data are the 100 counties of North Carolina, which
ship with the `sf` package, over 20 years.

## The model

Surveys report \(y\) positives out of \(k\) tested. Surveys in the same area
and time step are pooled into one *cell*. The number positive in cell
(area \(a\), time \(t\)) is binomial, with logit prevalence

\[
x_{at} = z_{at}^\top \beta + f_{at} + \epsilon_{at}.
\]

- \(z_{at}^\top \beta\) are fixed effects: an intercept, by default a linear
  trend, and any covariates.
- \(f\) is a Gaussian field with separable covariance.
  - In space it is a Leroux conditional autoregressive model on the
    adjacency graph of the areas, with scale \(\sigma\) and spatial
    dependence \(\rho_s\).
  - In time it is a first-order autoregression with correlation
    \(\rho_t\).
- \(\epsilon\) is a cell-level nugget with standard deviation
  \(\sigma_n\), for variation between surveys that the smooth field does not
  explain.

Most area-time cells have no data. Because the prior is Gaussian, those
cells can be integrated out exactly, and so can \(\beta\), so the sampler
works on the observed cells only. A fit to a few thousand observed cells
is then feasible, even when the full table has millions of cells. The
full surface is reconstructed afterwards, once per posterior draw.

## 1. The spatial frame

A frame holds the areas, their adjacency graph and any groupings to
aggregate to. It is built from polygons (or from an adjacency matrix, or
as a regular lattice with `areal_lattice()`). Here the counties are grouped
into three regions by longitude.

```{r frame}
library(stareal)
nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
lon <- sf::st_coordinates(suppressWarnings(sf::st_centroid(sf::st_geometry(nc))))[, 1]
nc$region <- cut(lon, 3, labels = c("west", "central", "east"))
fr <- areal_frame(nc, id = "FIPS", groups = c(county = "NAME", region = "region"))
fr
```

Areas sharing a border or a corner are neighbours. Islands, and any other
pieces of the graph cut off from the rest, are joined to the nearest
mainland area, so every area borrows strength from its neighbours.

## 2. The time frame

```{r time}
tf <- time_frame(2005, 2024, "year")
tf
```

## 3. Data

Real data are a table of surveys, each with a location (an area id, or
coordinates) and a date. `areal_data()` assigns each survey to an area
(by id, or by point in polygon, with points just outside every polygon
snapped to the nearest one) and to a time step, then pools the surveys
into cells. Every survey it cannot use is kept, with the reason:

```{r data-real, eval = FALSE}
d <- areal_data(surveys, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("lon", "lat"), date = "date")
d          # surveys used, cells, and every exclusion with its reason
```

Here the surveys are simulated from the model with known parameters:
300 county-years surveyed, 60 people tested in each. `simulate_areal()`
returns the same kind of object, with the truth attached.

```{r simulate}
sim <- simulate_areal(fr, tf, sigma = 1, rho_s = 0.9, rho_t = 0.8, sigma_n = 0.3,
                      beta = c(-1, 1.5), n_cells = 300, k = 60, seed = 42)
sim
head(sim$cells)
```

## 4. Fitting

The defaults of `mcmc_control()` are a pilot run. Here a short run keeps
the vignette quick; settings can be given as a plain list, and anything
left out takes its default. Chains run in parallel, one per worker
process.

```{r fit}
fit <- fit_areal(sim, control = list(n_iter = 1500, n_burn = 500, n_store = 200, n_chains = 2,
                                     ess_sweeps = 5, n_cores = 2, verbose = FALSE))
summary(fit)
sim$truth$theta
```

`plot(fit)` shows the traces. `diagnose()` checks convergence and mixing
for *every* parameter, including each observed cell's latent value.
Hyperparameters can look converged while the cells mix poorly, so a run
is only accepted when both are acceptable.

```{r diagnose}
dg <- diagnose(fit)
dg$checks
```

This short run fails the default thresholds (which are set for
publication), so a real analysis would run longer chains. For long fits,
give `fit_areal()` a `checkpoint_dir`: an interrupted fit, run again,
resumes where it stopped.

## 5. Prediction

`predict()` reconstructs the prevalence of every county in every year,
once per posterior draw. It then summarises each county-year, and
aggregates each draw to the regions before summarising. Because the
regional estimates come from joint draws, their uncertainty accounts for
the correlation between counties. Weights set each county's share of its
region; here they are births in 1974.

```{r predict}
pr <- predict(fit, groups = "region", weights = setNames(nc$BIR74, nc$FIPS),
              exceedance = 0.5, verbose = FALSE)
head(pr$area[, c("id", "county", "time", "y", "k", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5", "p_gt_0.5")])
```

With the truth known, the coverage of the 95% intervals can be checked:

```{r coverage}
truth <- sim$truth$prevalence[cbind(match(pr$area$id, fr$ids), pr$area$t)]
mean(pr$area$q2.5 <= truth & truth <= pr$area$q97.5)
```

```{r plots}
plot(pr, time = "2024")
plot(pr, time = "2024", stat = "p_gt_0.5")
plot(pr, group = "region")
head(pr$groups$region)
```

```{r series, fig.height = 5}
plot(pr)   # the best-surveyed counties, with their data
```

## 6. Covariates

Covariates are given as tables keyed by area (`id`), by time step (`t`
or `time`), or by both. They must cover every area and time step, since
predictions are made everywhere. Numeric covariates are standardised, so
their effects are per standard deviation. Priors on the fixed effects can
be named by design column, e.g. `priors = list(beta_sd = c(programmeon = 1))`.

```{r covariates}
covs <- list(data.frame(id = nc$FIPS, log_births = log(nc$BIR74)),
             data.frame(time = tf$labels, programme = ifelse(2005:2024 >= 2015, "on", "off")))
f_cov <- ~ trend() + log_births + programme
sim2 <- simulate_areal(fr, tf, formula = f_cov, covariates = covs, sigma = 0.8, rho_s = 0.9,
                       rho_t = 0.8, sigma_n = 0.3,
                       beta = c(-1, 1, 0.5, -0.7), n_cells = 300, k = 60, seed = 7)
fit2 <- fit_areal(sim2, formula = f_cov, covariates = covs,
                  control = list(n_iter = 1500, n_burn = 500, n_store = 200, n_chains = 2,
                                 ess_sweeps = 5, n_cores = 2, verbose = FALSE))
s <- summary(fit2)$table
s[s$type == "beta", c("variable", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")]
sim2$truth$beta
```

## 7. Cross-validation

`crossval()` holds out each fold of cells in turn, refits, and scores the
held-out cells. Compare models fitted to the same cells by the mean log
score (higher is better). About 5% of observations should fall outside
their 95% predictive interval. Each fold is a full refit:

```{r crossval, eval = FALSE}
cv <- crossval(fit, folds = 10)
cv$overall
```

## Scale

Two things set the cost:

- **The eigendecomposition of the graph.** `areal_frame()` does it once.
  It is a dense \(m \times m\) problem: seconds for hundreds of areas, a
  minute or so for a few thousand.
- **Each MCMC iteration.** It costs \(O(n^3)\) in the number of observed
  cells \(n\), because of a dense Cholesky factorisation.

The method was developed on about 1,300 and 1,800 observed cells. There,
a publication-length run takes a few hours with an optimised BLAS (Intel
MKL, OpenBLAS or Apple Accelerate). With R's reference BLAS it takes many
times longer. Prediction holds one block of areas at a time, so memory
stays bounded however many draws are used.
